name: Umar Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy fresh fruit, dried fruit and nuts for Meridian Fresh Foods, which supplies independent grocers and restaurants. My day starts at 5:30 with the market price sheets, because oranges can move overnight. By nine I'm on calls with growers in Turkey, Spain and Egypt, and then I check the weather, the ports and the cold store. Afternoons are for the trade customers who want to know why their pistachios cost more.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the smell of the cold store in September, and I love finding a small grower nobody has noticed. What wears me out is being the one who's blamed when a container sits at the port for nine days. My wife Zeynep, a pharmacist, says I talk to growers more than to her, and she may be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. I call this one "AI Plateau". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful assistant and not much more. At work I'd tell the team to use it for translating supplier emails and tidying price lists, and to keep their brains on the growers. To friends I'd say I told you so about the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be relieved. I'm 58 and I'd like my last years to be about oranges and ports, not about a restructure. The routine bits get faster, but the real work is knowing who to trust, and that stays human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd use the AI for first drafts of emails to Spanish growers, still check every figure myself, and keep up my union membership. I'd also keep my plan to retire at 63 and hand the grower contacts to Katya, my deputy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the version of the future I'd choose, because I know how to do my job and I'm paid well for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd carry on. What's weighing on you at Meridian right now, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pressure is the supermarkets. The chains squeeze our independent customers, and every year a couple of my best grocers close. If they go, my volumes go. Also freight costs and the weather, which AI doesn't fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to translate and draft, mostly, and sometimes to compare price lists from three growers. It's good at that. I'd never let it ring a grower in a bad season, because a grower with a sick harvest wants a person to hear it.

say: I'd tell the team it's a **useful assistant**, good for translating emails and tidying price lists.
I'd tell friends the **hype** was overdone.
think: Privately I'm relieved: my last years can stay about **growers** and ports.
The real work is knowing **who to trust**, and that stays human.
do: Keep using AI for **first drafts** to Spanish growers while checking every figure myself.
Keep my **union membership** and plan to retire at 63, handing contacts to Katya.
feel: **Calm**, because it's the future I'd choose and I'm paid well to do what I know.
S0.quote: I'd never let it ring a grower in a bad season, because a grower with a sick harvest wants a person to hear it.
fieldNote: Comfortable with the tools and clear about their **limits**.
His worry in this world is customers closing, not software.
Warm, storytelling voice built on trust with growers.

steps.text: Use AI for first drafts of emails to Spanish growers
Keep paying union dues and attending branch meetings
Keep ringing growers myself in bad seasons

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. I call this one "Steady Disruption". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the change is real and we should talk about it honestly. At work I'd say we should use these tools before someone uses them on us. To friends I'd say a good society makes sure the savings from software are shared, not pocketed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the price comparison and reordering go first. That's about half my week. Meridian may decide six buyers can become three, and I'd be one of the ones who decides who. That's not a nice thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly this winter, with a course Zeynep found me. I'd move my team onto the relationship side, the growers and the difficult customers, and let software do reorders. And I'd ask the union branch to open talks about retraining before a cut is announced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job is safe enough for now, but the ground is moving under my team, and I feel responsible for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your day would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Katya, my deputy, is brilliant but 36 and has two small children. If the team halves, I'd go to the owners and say, take my pay cut before you take Katya's job. I mean it. I've had the better years, and I have the cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your union branch or Meridian to do if the buying team shrank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for an agreement that no one in buying is let go in the first two years without a retraining offer and six months' notice. I'd also ask for a share of any savings to go into a training fund. It isn't radical, it's what any decent employer should do.

say: I'd say we should use these tools **before** someone uses them on us.
To friends I'd say the **savings** should be shared, not pocketed.
think: Privately I think **reordering and price checks** go first, about half my week.
Meridian might cut six buyers to three, and I'd help **decide** who.
do: Take a proper **AI course** this winter and move my team onto growers and difficult customers.
Ask the **union branch** to open retraining talks before any cut is announced.
feel: **Uneasy**, as my job looks safe but my team's ground is moving.
S1.quote: I'd go to the owners and say, take my pay cut before you take Katya's job. I mean it.
fieldNote: He volunteers to **sacrifice** pay to protect his deputy.
Safe himself, so the unease is about responsibility for others.
Turns to collective bargaining rather than personal escape.

steps.text: Take a proper AI course this winter
Shift my team onto grower and difficult-customer work
Ask the union branch for retraining talks before cuts
Offer a pay cut to the owners to protect Katya

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. I call this one "AGI by 2028". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and we need emergency rules now. At work I'd say let's keep calm and make a plan together. Online I'd call for public support for everyone whose work disappears, paid for by whoever profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job as it is today is gone by 2028. Anyone can ask the software to find the cheapest pistachios from five countries. What's left is the hand-shaking with growers, and I'm not sure that pays a salary. My wife's pharmacy work is safer, though not for long, because dispensing is partly rules and checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd put Meridian's owners and my union in one room. I'd look at our savings with Zeynep and decide to pay off the flat we rent out to my sister. Then I'd think about a move to a small import consultancy, helping small growers sell to Europe, which is the human part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have the money to survive but not the sense of purpose, and I'm not ready to be useless at 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is not long for you. What changes in your first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shareholders of the tech firms, and the governments who let it run without rules. I don't blame the machine. If a handful of companies earn everything, then the rest of us should be paid something back through tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write to my MP and join a march. I'd also help my daughter Ayla, a social worker, who will see the damage first. She'd have more people at her door than ever, and she has no cushion like mine.

say: I'd call for **emergency rules** and public support for everyone whose work disappears.
I'd tell the team to stay calm and **plan together**.
think: Privately my job as it stands is **gone by 2028**, and growers' trust may not pay a salary.
Zeynep's pharmacy work is safer, but only for a while.
do: Put the owners and the **union** in one room in month one.
Start planning a small **consultancy** helping small growers sell to Europe, and join a march.
feel: **Anxious**: money would carry us, but I'm not ready to feel useless at 60.
S2.quote: I don't blame the machine. If a handful of companies earn everything, then the rest of us should be paid something back through tax.
fieldNote: His **anxiety** is about purpose and the household, not about money.
Blames firms and governments, not the technology.
Already sketching a human-trust consultancy as an exit.

steps.text: Get the owners and union branch into one room
Sketch a consultancy helping small growers sell to Europe
Write to my MP and join a march
Support daughter Ayla through her busier social work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. I call this one "AGI by 2031". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare and short enough to be taken seriously. At work I'd push for a retraining plan. Online I'd say it's an opportunity if we share the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's more bearable. I'd be 63, close to my planned retirement, and I'd probably leave Meridian a year early with my pension. But I'd worry for Katya and the younger buyers, who have 25 years to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now, by taking Katya to every important grower meeting so she has the relationships when I go. I'd learn to use the AI tools in a serious way, since I'd rather be the one running them. And I'd invest a bit in my friend's small dried-fruit importing business, as an interest in my years after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's a waiting-room feeling, not a drowning one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you time. What would you do with the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be frantic. With five I can still teach, still save and still volunteer. I'd also help Zeynep think through her own pharmacy plans, because her job will change too. We both have the savings, so we can afford to be calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use that time with your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with Deniz, my son who's an engineer abroad, and ask what he sees at his firm. And I'd ask Ayla how her service would handle more people. We should have a family talk about it once a year, with food.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to **prepare** and short enough to be taken seriously.
Online I'd say it's an opportunity **if** we share the gains.
think: Privately I'd be near retirement at 63, so I'd likely leave a **year early**.
I'd worry for Katya, who has **25 years** to go.
do: Take Katya to every key **grower meeting** so she inherits the relationships.
Learn AI tools seriously and put a little money into my friend's small **importing business**.
feel: **Anxious** but with a plan, like sitting in a waiting room.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be frantic. With five I can still teach, still save and still volunteer.
fieldNote: Time converts his **anxiety** into planning and mentoring.
Mentoring Katya is his main goal, ahead of his own job.
Starts a modest investment in a friend's business.

steps.text: Take Katya to every key grower meeting this year
Learn to run the AI buying tools myself
Put some savings into a friend's dried-fruit import firm
Plan to retire a year early on full pension

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. I call this one "AGI by 2036". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade to build something fair. At work I'd say nothing changes this month, so let's learn. Online I'd say the planning should start now, because ten years goes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'll be retired by then, so it's less about me. It's about Deniz and Ayla and any grandchildren. I'd want them to have decent work and decent pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to 63, run a few mentoring evenings for young buyers, and use my savings to help each of my children buy a flat, if they want. And I'd put some money in index funds, because I believe the economy will do well even if jobs shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a mild, almost philosophical way. It's more curiosity than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you beyond retirement. Does it still matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 and probably walking in the hills with Zeynep. I'd also be involved with the union as a retired member, visiting the young. I'd want to be useful rather than bitter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want people to do in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want companies to be forced to retrain people with money and time, and governments to pay for it together. A decade is exactly enough to do that if we start soon. If we don't, we'll wake up in 2036 and be shocked.

say: I'd say ten years is a decade to **build something fair** if we start planning now.
At work I'd say nothing changes this month, so let's **keep learning**.
think: Privately I'll be retired by then, so it's about **Deniz and Ayla** and any grandchildren.
I believe the economy will do well even if **jobs shift**.
do: Work to **63** and run mentoring evenings for young buyers.
Help each of my children with a **flat deposit** if they want, and buy some index funds.
feel: **Uneasy**, but mild and curious, more philosophical than frightened.
S4.quote: A decade is exactly enough to do that if we start soon. If we don't, we'll wake up in 2036 and be shocked.
fieldNote: With ten years, his concern becomes **generational**: his children's work.
Optimistic about the economy, pessimistic about politics.
Money is a tool for his children, not a fear.

steps.text: Run mentoring evenings for young buyers until I retire
Help each child with a flat deposit
Buy index funds with spare savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most, because there is no time for fairness. What would help is a quick, honest talk between owners, unions and government, with retraining paid for by the firms that save money. I'd also like a clear pension guarantee for people my age. Give people time and a share, and most of us will adapt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people say 'adapt' as if it's easy. I adapt well, and I have savings, a good wife and a good job. Imagine everyone else who has none of those. I'd like policy to be written for them.

headlineQuote: I adapt well, and I have savings, a good wife and a good job. Imagine everyone else who has none of those.
portrait: Umar is a **58-year-old** senior buyer of fresh and dried fruit and nuts for a distributor serving independent grocers and restaurants.
He is a warm, progressive storyteller who uses **AI tools** now and then, for translating and price lists.
He stays calm if little changes, and grows more anxious as the timeline shortens, mostly about purpose and about his deputy Katya.
He blames tech firms, shareholders and governments, never the machine, and turns to the union and politics.
His savings and a pharmacist wife give him room to **mentor**, invest and help his children.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most because there is no time for fairness or retraining.
whatWouldHelp: A quick, honest talk between **owners, unions and government**, with retraining paid for by firms that save money, and a pension guarantee.
